analysis.one_liner: Bans the President, members of Congress, senior officials, and federal judges from owning or trading stocks, crypto, or prediction-market bets.
analysis.headline: Introduced in late August 2026 with zero cosponsors, the bill has sat in four House committees with no markup and no vote as the session winds down.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar the President, Vice President, members of Congress, senior executive officials, and federal judges — plus their spouses and dependent children — from owning or trading individual stocks, commodities, futures, digital assets, and prediction-market contracts. They would have 30 days to sell, could keep only broadly diversified index funds, Treasury bonds, and municipal bonds, and would face steep fines (up to 50% of the value of holdings kept in violation) plus forfeiture of any profits from banned trades. Ethics offices would publish every fine online. [S2]
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, who would no longer have lawmakers and officials with the power to write tax law, regulate industries, or award contracts holding stakes in the companies those decisions move. Government decisions would no longer sit alongside personal portfolios in the same companies. [S2]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Citizens relying on impartial government decisions

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the President, Vice President, members of Congress, senior officials, and federal judges, along with their spouses and dependent children, from owning or trading stocks, commodities, futures, digital assets, and prediction-market contracts. [S2]
Requires divestment within 30 days and allows only broadly diversified, publicly traded index funds, U.S. Treasuries, municipal bonds, small-business stakes, and a home-holding LLC. [S2]

Imposes real penalties: a daily fee of 10% of the value of noncompliant holdings (capped at 50%), forfeiture of the value of any banned trade plus $10,000, disgorgement of profits, subpoena power for ethics offices, collection from salary or pension, and mandatory public posting of every fine and its reason. [S2]
Bars paying any penalty with official funds, campaign contributions, or office allowances — violators must pay out of pocket. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Sitting lawmakers, senior executive officials, and federal judges, plus their families, who would have to sell individual stocks and crypto within 30 days — and because the bill overrides the normal tax deferral for forced divestitures, those sales would trigger immediate capital gains taxes. [S2]
analysis.who_pays_short: Lawmakers, judges, senior officials, their families

drawbacks.text: The bill expressly excludes the normal tax rule that defers capital gains tax when a federal law forces a divestment, so covered officials would owe immediate taxes on 30-day forced sales, potentially in a lump sum. [S2]

A spouse or dependent child who works in finance could keep trading covered investments as their primary occupation, so long as the assets are not owned by the covered official — a significant enforcement gap. [S2]

A good-faith objection: applying a near-total investment ban to every federal judge and a wide swath of senior officials, with 30-day deadlines and daily fines, could discourage qualified people from entering or staying in public service. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core ban targets a genuine conflict of interest — people voting on tax bills or regulating companies while holding those companies' stock — and the penalty structure is unusually concrete. The immediate capital gains tax on forced sales, the narrowness of what may be kept, and the spouse occupational exception are real design flaws an honest supporter would concede, but they are secondary to the central change.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with no cosponsors and referred to four House committees, none of which has taken it up, leaving it stalled with the session ending in early January. [S1, S3, S4]

narrative.text: Rep. Eugene Vindman introduced the bill on August 31, 2026, with no cosponsors. [S1, S3, S4]

It was referred simultaneously to four committees — Oversight and Government Reform, House Administration, Judiciary, and Ways and Means — for a period to be determined by the Speaker, splitting its consideration across panels. [S4]
No committee has scheduled a markup or hearing, and the bill has received no floor action. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Current officeholders — lawmakers, senior executive officials, and federal judges — are better off for now, since they keep the right to hold and trade individual stocks, crypto, and prediction-market bets that the bill would have stripped. [S2, S4]

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Officeholders who would have had to divest

for.name: Rep. Eugene Vindman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to four House committees.

against.name: Speaker of the House
against.role: House Speaker, controls committee referrals and floor scheduling
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred jointly to four committees for a period to be determined by the Speaker, splitting it across panels, and it has not been brought to the floor.

against.name: Chairs of Oversight, House Administration, Judiciary, and Ways and Means
against.role: Committee chairs with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: No committee has scheduled a markup, hearing, or vote since the bill was referred in late August 2026.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and the bill has zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split is visible in the record. [S3, S4]

industries.industry: Sitting federal officeholders (President, Vice President, members of Congress, senior executive officials, federal judges) and their families
industries.note: They would have to divest individual stocks, crypto, and event contracts within 30 days, forfeit profits from banned trades, and face daily fines up to 50% of noncompliant holdings. Their financial interest in keeping current rules runs directly against the public's interest in officials without personal stakes in their own decisions. [S2]

industries.industry: Brokerages and digital-asset and prediction-market platforms
industries.note: They would lose a small class of customers — officials barred from trading their products, with crypto and event contracts expressly covered. The interest in keeping this trading channel open runs against the reform's purpose. [S2]

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and referral to four committees, the bill is very unlikely to get a markup before the Congress ends on January 3, 2027. Most one-sponsor, no-cosponsor bills at this stage expire quietly when the session closes. [S3, S4]
